title: Davenant’s triple ‘mortal’: irremissible Spirit-sin; remissible kingdom-barring guilt
source_text: XXX. Notandum est, inquit, peccatum dici posse mortale, vel mortiferum tripliciter. Primo quod trahit secum meritum aeternae mortis absolutum, certum, & irrevocabile. Hoc sensu peccatum in Spiritum Sanctum solummodo habetur mortale. Secundo usitate vocatur mortale peccatum quod peccantem involvit reatu mortis aeternae, sed remissibili, quodque illum partem in regno Dei habere non sinit, donec per poenitentiam ad vitam redeat. Hujusmodi sunt illa omnia quae recensentur ab Apostolo 1 Cor. 6. Nolite errare, neque fornicatores, &c. regnum Dei possidebunt. Eadem doctrina Galat. 5. repetitur, Manifesta sunt opera carnis, quae sunt adulterium, fornicatio, &c. qui talia agunt regnum Dei non consequentur.
pass_a_gloss: It is to be noted, he says, that sin can be called mortal or death-bringing in a threefold way. First, that which draws with it an absolute, certain, and irrevocable desert of eternal death. In this sense only the sin against the Holy Spirit is held mortal. Second, sin is commonly called mortal which involves the sinner in the guilt of eternal death, but remissible, and which does not suffer him to have a part in the kingdom of God until by repentance he returns to life. Of this kind are all those which are rehearsed by the Apostle in 1 Cor. 6: Be not deceived; neither fornicators, etc., shall possess the kingdom of God. The same doctrine is repeated in Galatians 5: The works of the flesh are manifest, which are adultery, fornication, etc.; they who do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God.
pass_b_english: Davenant’s first mortal: only the Spirit-sin’s irrevocable death-desert.
Second: remissible yet kingdom-barring guilt—Paul’s flesh-work catalogs until repentance restores life.

choices.why: Second sense is ordinary theological speech.
